newsitem.title: USA: Online merchants ring in holiday sales.
newsitem.headline: Online merchants ring in holiday sales.

text.p: It's shaping up to be a very merry Christmas for online stores.

Web-based merchants and shops on online services such as America Online report booming sales of everything from slippers to teddy bears to personal electronics. Some online retailers have seen sales jump 30 percent in the past 30 days, and others are registering record numbers of visitors to their virtual stores.
America Online, which welcomed a surge of new users after adopting flat-fee pricing on Dec. 1, hit $1 million in merchandise sales Saturday (Dec. 7), a record for the online service.
"It bodes well for the season for electronic commerce," said Michael Minigan, head of AOL's interactive commerce division.

It does indeed. In November, technology researcher International Data Corp. estimated online sales of goods and services during the all-important four-week shopping period between Thanksgiving and Christmas would hit $150 million, fuelled in part by newcomers jumping onto the Net.

That's a mere drop in the bucket compared with holiday sales through traditional retailers and direct marketers. But it represents a giant leap forward from last year, when consumers intent on doing their Christmas shopping online found a handful of stores offering limited inventory, and more often than not, no online ordering.

This year, services such as Infoseek's Holiday Ultrashop (http://204.183.199.77/) shopping catalogue and Your Personal Network's shopping guide (http://www.ypn.com/shopping) list thousands of online merchants and malls offering the gamut of electronics, apparel, sporting goods, food, books and other gift items. At most shops, online ordering is de rigeur, as are other interactive amenities including electronic shopping carts, in-site search engines and concierges who make gift suggestions via e-mail.

"Every store you'd find at any strip mall in America has a storefront on the Net," said Jay Sears, marketing vice president of Wolff New Media, publisher of Your Personal Network and "NetShopping" a new book about online stores. "What you're seeing is the first Internet Christmas."

And oh, what a Christmas. iQVC, the TV shopping network's Web site (http://www.iqvc.com/), registered $1 million in sales in the past 30 days, with shoppers zeroing in on teddy bears, jewelry, personal electronics, collectibles and kitchen wares, said Stuart Spiegel, the site's general manager.
"We really decked the halls. We trimmed the windows, we look like the holiday season, and consumers are reacting," Spiegel said.
So much business had some unexpected consequences: iQVC needed to add firepower -- more computer hardware and software -- to its Web site to keep it from overloading and freezing out would-be buyers.
"We're chasing it as fast as we can," Spiegel said.

Booksellers also report strong sales. Charles Stack, owner of Book Stacks Unlimited (http://www.books.com/), the Cleveland-based online bookstore, said sales are up 30 percent over the past month, and gift-book sales have tripled.
"People are more accustomed to purchasing online, and more comfortable. In the past it was more of a novelty," Stack said.
At rival Amazon.com (http://www.amazon.com/), sales have risen faster than usual during recent weeks, but a representative of the Seattle-based online bookseller wouldn't provide other details.

All's well at L.L. Bean, the venerable mail-order marketer, which revamped its year-old Web site for the holidays. The site (http://www.llbean.com/), which formerly directed shoppers to call or e-mail for a print catalogue, now offers 300 items for sale online. Chamois shirts and "Wicked Good" slippers are early standouts, said Linh Calhoun, a company spokeswoman.

At America Online, shoppers can browse through 50 stores in the online Marketplace or buy merchandise in 350 other content areas. Best-selling products include computers, software, CD-ROMs, modems and branded merchandise from Eddie Bauer, Land's End, J.C. Penney and Hanes, said Minigan, who heads AOL's interactive-commerce division.
"Based on the early start we got (over Thanksgiving weekend), we should double what we did last year for the comparable period," Minigan said.
So much of the holiday shopping experience has come online, shoppers can even find Christmas fruitcake, of the virtual variety.

Visitors to the Internet Florist (http://www.virtualflorist.com/) can send a colour picture of a fruitcake to anyone with an e-mail address, at no charge. The St. Paul, Minn.-based company has delivered 30,000 of the virtual victuals in the past two weeks, and tens of thousands more virtual bouquets to promote its real-life Web-based flower delivery business.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
